title: I replaced learning apps with Gemini Guided Learning; it remembers my progress and adapts to my pace
excerpt: I deleted half my learning apps; it made learning surprisingly addictive
content_html:
Published Nov 14, 2026, 3:00 PM EST

I cover Android with a focus on productivity, automation, and Google’s ecosystem, including Gemini and everyday apps. With a background in engineering and software development, I tend to go beyond surface-level tips.
Before joining AP, I wrote for tech publications such as Gizbot in 2023 and iJunkie (formerly known as iPhoneHacks) from 2021 to 2022.

Learning on my phone used to feel unnecessarily complicated. I'd jump between YouTube videos, articles, notes, and course apps when I wanted to understand something new.

Still, I felt like I wasn't making progress. The material lived across apps on my phone, and keeping track of where I left off took more effort than the learning itself.

I wanted an easier way to stay on track without juggling multiple tools.

That's when I stumbled into Guided Learning, a Gemini feature I'd mostly been ignoring, and slowly realized I was opening my learning apps less and less.

Why I kept quitting learning apps

I kept forgetting where I left off

I kept downloading learning apps, thinking they'd make me more productive or help me pick up new skills faster.

At first, everything seemed fine. The courses were well-designed, and the progress bars made me feel like I was moving forward.

But after a few days, the shine wore off. Each app demanded its own attention. Where did I leave off? Was I ready for the next lesson, or should I revisit the last one?

Sometimes a topic would spread across multiple sources. I would hop between tabs, copy and paste notes, and try to remember what I'd learned.

By the end of the week, I'd often give up.

Guided Learning in Gemini solved the problem

It guided me step by step, building on what I learned

Everything changed when I started using Gemini's Guided Learning feature.

Unlike traditional learning apps, it didn't need me to follow a rigid path or track progress across multiple tools.

Instead, it guided me step by step, building on what I already knew and adjusting as I went. I didn't have to plan my learning sessions or decide which topic to tackle next.

Guided Learning remembered where I left off and suggested the next logical step. If I paused for a few days, I could pick up where I left off without needing to figure out the context.

It also made mistakes and gaps useful. When I misunderstood a concept, Guided Learning explained why I made the mistake and how to approach similar problems in the future.

The best part was flexibility. I could proceed at my pace, skip sections I understood, or explore topics I found interesting, without switching between multiple apps or tutorials.

How I use Guided Learning in Gemini

I just tell Gemini what I want to learn

I don't open Gemini with a syllabus in mind. Most of the time, I start with a vague goal and a rough sense of what I want to understand next.

Guided Learning works best when I treat it like a conversation, rather than a lesson I have to finish in one sitting.

One example of this was learning the basics of self-hosting.

I wasn't trying to become a sysadmin overnight; I just wanted to understand what it would take to run a few services on my hardware.

Instead of searching for a self-hosting beginner course, I asked Gemini to start a guided learning path focused on the fundamentals.

To get started, open a new chat in the Gemini mobile app or on the web and tap the Add Files. Select Guided Learning and input the topic you wish to explore.

From there, the topic was divided into manageable sections, beginning with concepts such as the meaning of self-hosting, the trade-offs when compared to cloud services, and the types of hardware that are suitable for beginners.

As I asked follow-up questions, Guided Learning automatically adjusted the depth.

I liked how easy it was to pause and resume. I'd read through a step, close the app, and come back later without feeling lost.

Guided Learning remembered the context and continued from there, rather than resetting the conversation or forcing me to repeat myself.

Tips to get more out of Guided Learning

Pop quizzes are a great way to test your knowledge

One of the simplest ways to better understand the topic is to ask for quick check-ins along the way.

If I'm not sure whether something has sunk in, I prompt Gemini to quiz me on the last concept or to give me a couple of short questions before moving on.

It's an easy way to catch gaps early, instead of realizing later that I only half understood what I read.

Follow-up questions matter just as much. When something feels unclear, I ask about it immediately.

Guided Learning adjusts based on those interruptions, often rephrasing the explanation or adding context that makes the rest of the path easier to follow.

I also try to end sessions with a lightweight recap. Asking for a summary of what I've covered helps reinforce the key ideas and makes it easier to resume learning.

On days when I don't have time to continue, that recap becomes a natural stopping point.

Where Guided Learning falls short

The examples and analogies can get boring

Guided Learning isn't perfect, and its biggest weakness shows up when you spend enough time with it.

Gemini relies heavily on examples and analogies, especially when it explains unfamiliar concepts. That can be helpful at first, but over time it starts to feel repetitive.

Different ideas are compared to the same kinds of real-world scenarios, which can slow things down when you're past the beginner stage.

It also tends to over-explain. Even when I'm comfortable with a topic, Guided Learning sometimes insists on walking through familiar ground, framing it with another analogy instead of moving on.

Another limitation is depth. Guided Learning is good at building understanding, but it's not always the fastest way to get highly specific or technical answers.

When I want exact commands, edge cases, or detailed troubleshooting, I sometimes have to switch out of guided mode and ask more direct questions instead.

While context awareness is a big part of the appeal, it can occasionally feel too cautious.

Gemini often tries to make sure you're "ready" before advancing, which is helpful early on but can feel restrictive when you're comfortable moving faster.

A better way to keep learning

Guided Learning works for me because it removes the setup that usually gets in the way of learning something new.

I didn't have to pick the right app, commit to a course, or remember where I left off.

However, it isn't flawless. Gemini can over-explain, and it sometimes needs a push to get past familiar ground.

But those are trade-offs I'm willing to make for something that adapts to my pace.

I also try to end sessions with a lightweight recap. Asking for a summary of what I've covered helps reinforce the key ideas and makes it easier to resume learning.

On days when I don't have time to continue, that recap becomes a natural stopping point.

Where Guided Learning falls short

The examples and analogies can get boring

Guided Learning isn't perfect, and its biggest weakness shows up when you spend enough time with it.

Gemini relies heavily on examples and analogies, especially when it explains unfamiliar concepts. That can be helpful at first, but over time it starts to feel repetitive.

Different ideas are compared to the same kinds of real-world scenarios, which can slow things down when you're past the beginner stage.

It also tends to over-explain. Even when I'm comfortable with a topic, Guided Learning sometimes insists on walking through familiar ground, framing it with another analogy instead of moving on.

Another limitation is depth. Guided Learning is good at building understanding, but it's not always the fastest way to get highly specific or technical answers.

When I want exact commands, edge cases, or detailed troubleshooting, I sometimes have to switch out of guided mode and ask more direct questions instead.

While context awareness is a big part of the appeal, it can occasionally feel too cautious.

Gemini often tries to make sure you're "ready" before advancing, which is helpful early on but can feel restrictive when you're comfortable moving faster.

A better way to keep learning

Guided Learning works for me because it removes the setup that usually gets in the way of learning something new.

I didn't have to pick the right app, commit to a course, or remember where I left off.

However, it isn't flawless. Gemini can over-explain, and it sometimes needs a push to get past familiar ground.

But those are trade-offs I'm willing to make for something that adapts to my pace.
